title.value: Child- and Proxy-reported Differences in Patient-reported Outcome and Experience Measures in Pediatric Surgery: Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
title.justification: The title is taken directly from the document header where it is clearly labeled as the review article's title.
title.quote: Child- and Proxy-reported Differences in Patient-reported Outcome and Experience Measures in Pediatric Surgery: Systematic Review and Meta-analysis

analysis.description: This paper conducts a systematic review and meta-analysis to compare child- and proxy-reported health outcomes in pediatric surgery using Patient-Reported Outcome Measures (PROMs) and Patient-Reported Experience Measures (PREMs). It highlights discrepancies between child and parent reports, the high heterogeneity in results across different measures, and insists on the need to consider both perspectives in pediatric health assessments.

type.justification: The paper involves a systematic review and a meta-analysis of empirical studies comparing outcomes and experiences as reported by children and their proxies.
type.quote: This review compares child-reported health status and treatment experiences from Patient-Reported Outcome Measures (PROMs) and Patient-Reported Experience Measures (PREMs) with parent reports.

name.justification: The research focuses on assessing health outcomes and experiences using informatics tools like PROMs and PREMs, which is a subset of health informatics.
name.quote: Despite the increasing implementation of PROMS and PREMs in clinical settings, their widespread use remains limited, particularly in pediatric surgery.

name.justification: The study is directly focused on patient-reported measures specific to surgical interventions in pediatric populations.
name.quote: Pediatric health outcomes are often assessed using proxy reports, which may not fully capture children's experiences. Children with surgical conditions face unique, changing healthcare journeys, making accurate representation challenging.

name.justification: PedsQLTM was the specific dataset used for a major portion of the analysis, as 22 studies with PedsQLTM data were included in the meta-analysis.
name.quote: PedsQLTM appeared in 30 studies, with 16 other quality of life measures used less frequently.

referenced_paper_title.value: Validity and responsiveness of the pediatric quality of life inventory (PedsQL) 4.0 generic core scales in the pediatric inpatient setting.
referenced_paper_title.justification: The authors referenced the paper to validate the use of PedsQLTM in their studies.
